subject: Triple-path connectivity options for Novaterra private deployment

From: Samuel Keller <samuel.keller@novaterra.com>

Subject: Connecting Novaterra VPC — which path should we pick?

Hi Irene,

Thanks for the quick chat earlier. We’re progressing the architecture for onboarding Novaterra onto Redwood Private (VPC-hosted control plane + our VPC in their account). Before we lock anything in, infra wanted a concise recommendation: for private connectivity between our infra and Novaterra’s VPC — is VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints + endpoint service), or a site-to-site VPN the right default?

Key constraints and context:
- We will process regulated PII and need clear auditability (SOC2 + data residency controls).
- Target p99 latency from Novaterra app to inference endpoints <50ms for most regions (us-east-1 primary).
- Cross-account pattern (Redwood in our account, Novaterra in theirs) and multi-AZ.
- Ops team wants minimal day-to-day maintenance on their side; they prefer managed endpoint acceptance flows over heavy BGP/routing changes if possible.
- They also want to understand failover patterns (multi-region) and how traffic egress is controlled.

Can you provide a short tradeoffs list and a recommended default pattern for us? If you need traffic profile numbers I can get those from their SREs.

Would appreciate a one-page summary we can attach to our internal RFC.

Thanks —
Sam
Samuel Keller
Head of Infrastructure, Novaterra

Sam — thanks, good prompt. Looping in Rishi (solutions arch) and Kimberly (security/product) so you get the config + compliance lens. High-level quick guidance below; Rishi will follow up with a compact matrix and a draft ops pattern we typically use.

Short answer (TL;DR):
- PrivateLink-first for strict tenant isolation + easiest cross-account security model.
- VPC Peering if you need the absolute lowest hop/latency inside a single region and are comfortable with cross-account route management.
- Site-to-site VPN only if you have on-prem constraints or cannot accept endpoint service architecture; it’s the lowest-friction but highest-variance for latency and observability.

Quick bullets (high level):
- Security/compliance: PrivateLink isolates traffic into an endpoint service, so Novaterra keeps control of the VPC-to-endpoint path and we don’t need to touch their VPC routes. That’s usually cleaner for audits.
- Latency: Peering typically beats PrivateLink by a small margin (single-region intra-VPC), but PrivateLink often meets sub-50ms p99 depending on AZ placement and NLB configuration. VPN latency is the least predictable.
- Ops: PrivateLink requires accepting interface endpoints (Novaterra) and maintaining an endpoint service (us) on our side. Peering requires cross-account peering request + route table changes — heavier ops for customers who want low-touch.
- Scale & availability: PrivateLink endpoints scale via NLB/endpoint-service; peering depends on instance sizing and pathing, VPNs need redundant tunnels for HA.

I’m attaching our latest network diagram (v2) that shows the endpoint service and peering fallback pattern — please share your expected request volume and p50/p95 sizes and we’ll run capacity recommendations.

Next steps I propose:
1) Rishi to send a one-page tradeoff matrix + estimated latency ranges and config checklist (NLB vs ALB, TLS termination, IP addressing).
2) Novaterra to provide request-per-second and typical payload sizes, and confirm if they want TLS mutual auth or are OK with TLS+mTLS at the app layer.
3) Tech design review (30–45m) with Novaterra infra next week to sign off on routing ownership and cutover plan.

If that sounds good I’ll tentatively schedule the review.

— Irene

Subject: Re: Connecting Novaterra VPC — which path should we pick? (tradeoff matrix)

Hey team — attaching a concise matrix (also pasted below). See attachment for SLA/impact numbers. High-level guidance and concrete configuration notes follow.

Attachment: sla-impact-matrix.xlsx (Excel, 38KB)

Tradeoff matrix (summary):
- VPC Peering:
  - Security: Good (VPC-level), but cross-account route entries are required; isolation depends on route tables and security groups.
  - Latency: Best (p50 ~6–12ms intra-region), very stable within same AZ pairing.
  - Ops: Higher friction for cross-account peering requests and route management; potential for accidental wide-scope routing if not careful.
  - Cost: Minimal data-transfer cost for most architectures (some inter-AZ charges).
  - Multi-region: Requires separate peering connections; more complexity.

- AWS PrivateLink (Interface endpoints + endpoint service):
  - Security: Best for tenant isolation and auditability; endpoint network interfaces are owned by Novaterra, we expose a service in our account. Least privileged from an audit standpoint.
  - Latency: Slightly higher than peering due to NLB hop, but generally within your 50ms p99 target in the same region (p50 ~10–18ms, p95 ~20–35ms depending on AZ alignment).
  - Ops: Low customer ops surface — accept endpoint, configure DNS, monitor endpoint health. On Redwood side, we need a highly available NLB + endpoint service and autoscaling knobs.
  - Cost: Endpoint hourly + data processing charges on top of NLB costs; can be material at high sustained bandwidth.
  - Multi-region: Works per-region; for multi-region failover we expose services in each region and control routing on the Novaterra side (DNS or weighted endpoints).

- Site-to-site VPN:
  - Security: Good if tunnels are properly configured; harder to show tenant-level separation in an audit compared to PrivateLink.
  - Latency: Least predictable (p50 ~30–60ms, can spike to 100ms+ depending on internet path).
  - Ops: Easiest to stand up quickly, but requires customer to manage VPN tunnels and BGP (if used) or static routes. Requires monitoring for tunnel flaps.
  - Cost: Lower hourly infra cost but potential higher egress/overhead due to encryption and intermediate hops.

Concrete recommendations for Novaterra (given your constraints):
1) Default pattern: PrivateLink in primary region + optional VPC Peering in the same region as a low-latency fallback for critical low-latency paths.
   - Rationale: PrivateLink gives the auditability and minimal-customer-ops preference you expressed; peering is available as an optimization if you need sub-20ms p99 for a narrow set of endpoints.
2) Endpoint configuration notes (PrivateLink):
   - Use an NLB fronting our inference fleet (TLS passthrough at NLB). Terminate TLS at the Redwood app nodes.
   - Recommend TCP keepalive and connection pooling to reduce connection churn at endpoints.
   - DNS: Novaterra should create a private hosted zone with CNAMEs to the interface endpoint IPs; use health checks for failover.
   - IAM & acceptance: We will use endpoint service acceptance workflow; Novaterra will create interface endpoints in their account and send acceptance.
3) Routing/ownership:
   - Novaterra owns endpoint creation and route table updates for their VPC. Redwood will provide the endpoint-service ARN and NLB details and support acceptance automation.
4) Observability & audit:
   - We’ll enable flow logs on the NLB and capture flow-level metrics in our observability console for audit traces.
5) Cost guardrails:
   - If Novaterra expects sustained >2Gbps traffic, we should revisit and possibly recommend peering for specific high-throughput subnets; otherwise PrivateLink’s simplicity outweighs the steady-state costs.

If Novaterra prefers minimal monthly bill variance and can do routing ops, peering-first is also defensible — but that increases their operational ownership and surface area for audit questions.

I can convert this into a one-pager for your RFC.

— Rishi

Thanks Rishi — that matrix is perfect. A couple quick clarifying items before the design review:
1) Traffic profile: initial phase 400–600 RPS average, p95 payload size ~600 bytes; expected bursts up to 1800 RPS during peak processing windows.
2) For the PrivateLink + peering hybrid you suggested, who owns the cutover orchestration on the day we enable peering? Novaterra SRE or Redwood on-call? We’d prefer Redwood to own the peering request and acceptance for the pilot, then hand over routing control to our team post-cutover.
3) Cost request: can you give a ballpark monthly delta for PrivateLink at 600–1800 RPS (assume 50% cache hit rate at edge) vs peering? We just need top-level numbers for our RFC.

If you can put those numbers in the one-pager and propose 3 optional windows for a 45m design review (Thu 10–11am PT, Fri 2–3pm PT, Mon 9–10am PT) we’ll pick and invite our infra folks.
